questions.q: In his last years of illness Maulana Wahiduddin Khan would answer, “I am alright.” How does the writer explain his calm?
options: He had stopped thinking about the future
Not quite. The article says: He lived in constant remembrance of God and of Paradise, which lifted him above worldly troubles.
He lived in constant remembrance of God and of Paradise, which lifted him above worldly troubles
Yes. The beauty of nature gave the writer a glimpse of the same.
He did not wish to trouble his doctors
Not quite. The article says: He lived in constant remembrance of God and of Paradise, which lifted him above worldly troubles.
His illness was not serious
Not quite. The article says: He lived in constant remembrance of God and of Paradise, which lifted him above worldly troubles.
questions.rationale: “He lived in constant remembrance of God and the eternal Paradise that awaits us beyond the confines of this world.”

questions.q: How does the article contrast the laws of this universe with those of the Hereafter?
options: Here there are no limits; there are many
Not quite. The article says: Here everything moves towards decay and is bound by limits of time and distance; there, existence is lasting and those limits fall away.
Both follow exactly the same laws
Not quite. The article says: Here everything moves towards decay and is bound by limits of time and distance; there, existence is lasting and those limits fall away.
Here nothing changes; there everything decays
Not quite. The article says: Here everything moves towards decay and is bound by limits of time and distance; there, existence is lasting and those limits fall away.
Here everything moves towards decay and is bound by limits of time and distance; there, existence is lasting and those limits fall away
Right. “The earth shall be changed into another earth.”
questions.rationale: “The Law of Entropy dictates that everything in this universe moves toward decay… the Quran describes a different set of laws in the Hereafter—the Law of Eternity.”

questions.q: What does the article give as the true purpose of education?
options: To gain a title
Not quite. The article says: To create awareness – the ability to understand issues and judge what is attainable – not merely to find a job.
To win arguments
Not quite. The article says: To create awareness – the ability to understand issues and judge what is attainable – not merely to find a job.
To create awareness – the ability to understand issues and judge what is attainable – not merely to find a job
Yes. Knowledge, not the sword, is now the key to strength.
To escape manual work
Not quite. The article says: To create awareness – the ability to understand issues and judge what is attainable – not merely to find a job.
questions.rationale: “The purpose of education is not only to find jobs; instead, its true purpose is to foster awareness within individuals.”

questions.q: Which phrase sums up the new outlook the article describes?
options: “Wait for better times”
Not quite. The article says: “Forget the past, educate the children”.
“Protest first, study later”
Not quite. The article says: “Forget the past, educate the children”.
“Forget the past, educate the children”
Well read. Dwelling on grievance was found to be futile.
“Remember the past, avenge the wrongs”
Not quite. The article says: “Forget the past, educate the children”.
questions.rationale: “This modern trend can be summed up in the following phrase: ‘Forget the past, educate the children.’”

questions.q: What parallel does the article draw between the forbidden tree and Ramadan?
options: Both are punishments
Not quite. The article says: Both are training in self-restraint – holding back from what is desired in order to build discipline.
Both are training in self-restraint – holding back from what is desired in order to build discipline
Correct. The first “training platform.”
Both concern particular foods
Not quite. The article says: Both are training in self-restraint – holding back from what is desired in order to build discipline.
Both apply only to prophets
Not quite. The article says: Both are training in self-restraint – holding back from what is desired in order to build discipline.
questions.rationale: “Just as Adam and Eve were asked to refrain from the tree as a test of discipline, we are asked to refrain from eating, drinking, and other desires during Ramadan.”

questions.q: The article says that today “our fingers are more restless than our appetites.” What does it recommend during Ramadan?
options: A digital fast as well – limiting phones and social media to make room for worship, reflection and family
Yes. It calls this “dopamine fasting.”
Using phones only at night
Not quite. The article says: A digital fast as well – limiting phones and social media to make room for worship, reflection and family.
Giving up fasting from food
Not quite. The article says: A digital fast as well – limiting phones and social media to make room for worship, reflection and family.
Following more religious accounts online
Not quite. The article says: A digital fast as well – limiting phones and social media to make room for worship, reflection and family.
questions.rationale: “This underscores the urgent need for not just a physical fast but a digital fast as well.”

questions.q: Which saying of the Prophet does the article quote to show that caring for the earth is a duty in every circumstance?
options: Plant only what you yourself will eat
Not quite. The article says: If the Hour is about to come and you have a sapling in your hand, plant it.
If the Hour is about to come and you have a sapling in your hand, plant it
Right. Planting a tree is also called a continuing charity.
Trees should be cut before they grow old
Not quite. The article says: If the Hour is about to come and you have a sapling in your hand, plant it.
Land belongs to whoever clears it
Not quite. The article says: If the Hour is about to come and you have a sapling in your hand, plant it.
questions.rationale: “If the Hour (of Judgement) is about to be established, and one of you has a sapling in his hand, let him plant it.”

questions.q: According to the article, what purpose do the imperfections and hardships of this world serve?
options: They humble us, turn us to God, and awaken a longing for the perfect world of Paradise
Yes. They are “not a flaw but a feature.”
They show that life has no purpose
Not quite. The article says: They humble us, turn us to God, and awaken a longing for the perfect world of Paradise.
They exist only as punishment
Not quite. The article says: They humble us, turn us to God, and awaken a longing for the perfect world of Paradise.
They are accidents with no meaning
Not quite. The article says: They humble us, turn us to God, and awaken a longing for the perfect world of Paradise.
questions.rationale: “The imperfections of this world exist to awaken in us the desire for Paradise—a realm of ultimate perfection.”

questions.q: Why does the article say reconciliation usually has to be one-sided, and why is it still worth it?
options: Both sides’ wishes rarely match, so one must give way – and this frees time and energy for constructive work
Exactly. Confrontation halts all such work.
It never works – so it should be avoided
Not quite. The article says: Both sides’ wishes rarely match, so one must give way – and this frees time and energy for constructive work.
Both sides always agree at once – so no effort is needed
Not quite. The article says: Both sides’ wishes rarely match, so one must give way – and this frees time and energy for constructive work.
The weaker side is always forced to yield – and gains nothing
Not quite. The article says: Both sides’ wishes rarely match, so one must give way – and this frees time and energy for constructive work.
questions.rationale: “In most cases, reconciliation requires a unilateral approach… it avoids unnecessary energy and time spent in wrangling, allowing for constructive action.”

questions.article: Woman at the Beginning of All Great Things
questions.q: What quality above all does the article say a woman needs to play the part Edison’s mother played?
options: Wealth
Not quite. The article says: Patience.
Higher education
Not quite. The article says: Patience.
Influence
Not quite. The article says: Patience.
Patience
Well read. The capability is given; its price is patience.
questions.rationale: “The most excellent quality required for this job is patience. The Creator creates the capability, but the person concerned must pay the price of patience.”
